title: Original Star Wars Hits IMAX for Its 50th Anniversary in 2027
summary:
In 1977, Star Wars changed cinema forever. Now, 50 years later, the original film is getting the ultimate upgrade: its first-ever IMAX release. Disney and Lucasfilm are bringing George Lucas's legendary space opera to IMAX screens in early 2027, just before the official anniversary on May 25.

According to Space.com, the newly restored print will screen at official IMAX locations starting February 19, 2027. Depending on the theater, audiences can watch it in either digital or physical film format. A limited number of IMAX 70mm sites will show the movie on actual film — a rare experience that preserves the original cinematic texture. The restoration reportedly strips away the "A New Hope" subtitle, the Special Edition alterations, and the CGI enhancements added in later years. That means Han Solo will once again shoot first in his famous confrontation with Greedo.

But the celebration doesn't stop there. A brand-new Star Wars movie, Star Wars: Starfighter, blasts off on May 28, 2027, over the anniversary weekend. Directed by Shawn Levy (known for Stranger Things and Deadpool & Wolverine), the film stars Ryan Gosling as Kade Auberon, a cynical rogue confronted by his mysterious past. The cast also includes Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Aaron Pierre, and Amy Adams.

Starfighter was shot with certified IMAX-approved digital cameras framed for IMAX screen ratios, then converted to IMAX 70mm film prints for exclusive venues in the U.S. This dual release strategy — a restored classic alongside a new adventure — gives fans two very different ways to celebrate five decades of lightsabers, Jedi, and the Force.

Whether you're a lifelong fan or a curious newcomer, 2027 promises to be a monumental year for Star Wars on the biggest screens imaginable.
why_it_matters: It shows how studios turn nostalgia into a business model, while also raising a real film-history question: whether audiences should see a classic the way it was originally shown, and whether physical film screenings can survive in a digital era.

background_read: Star Wars opened on May 25, 1977 and became a worldwide phenomenon; it was created by George Lucas, the American filmmaker who built the Star Wars universe and founded the studio Lucasfilm.

The original film's effects were made by Industrial Light & Magic, a company Lucas set up to build the spaceships and laser battles — it became one of the most influential special-effects studios in Hollywood.

Lucas later re-edited the trilogy for the 1997 Special Editions, adding computer-generated scenes and changing the famous Greedo confrontation; fans have argued ever since about which version counts as the 'real' film.
Disney now owns Lucasfilm, and IMAX is a large-format cinema company known for screens several storeys tall.

Real 70mm film prints are increasingly rare because most cinemas switched to digital projectors, so screenings on actual film are treated as special events — and old films often need restoration because film stock fades, scratches and changes colour over time.

perspectives.description: For the first time in decades fans can watch the 1977 film on giant screens, and a limited number can see it on genuine 70mm film. The restoration also restores the original cut, including Han Solo shooting first, which many fans consider the authentic version.

The anniversary is also a commercial event: Disney owns Lucasfilm and is pairing a re-release with a brand-new film to maximise ticket sales. Critics may argue the 'original version' debate is being used to sell the same film yet again.

Anniversary re-releases are a long-standing Hollywood practice, and format upgrades such as IMAX, 3D and remastered sound have repeatedly been used to bring old titles back to cinemas. Physical film screenings are now prestige events aimed at dedicated fans rather than ordinary audiences.

If the IMAX run performs well, other studios may restore more classics for large formats. The reception of Starfighter, shot with IMAX-approved cameras, may also shape how future Star Wars films are made and where they premiere.
